newsitem.title: USA: Chevron challenges Florida offshore drilling ban. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Chevron challenges Florida offshore drilling ban. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]

text.p: Spurred on by discovery of a huge natural gas field off Florida's Gulf coast, Chevron Corp. is mounting the latest challenge to a longstanding moratorium on offshore oil and natural gas production.

Federal regulators this week began poring over a detailed drilling plan submitted by Chevron U.S.A. Production Co., a Chevron subsidiary seeking approval to tap into a geological formation believed to be part of the largest natural gas play on the continent.

The U.S. Minerals Management Service, which regulates drilling in federal waters of the Gulf of Mexico, also plans Thursday to open a branch office in Pensacola, Fla., to handle what some expect will be a firestorm of protest against Chevron's drilling plans.

"Oil and gas drilling is extremely bad for the environment and it would issue a devastating blow to the economy of Florida," said Dan Jacobson of the Florida Public Interest Research Group. "It's just a risk that's not worth taking."

Chevron last Wednesday sought federal approval to produce natural gas lying under Destin Dome, a gas field about 25 miles south of Pensacola. The dome lies along the eastern edge of the Norphlet Trend, a geologic formation believed to hold up to 17 trillion cubic feet of gas.
"(The Norphlet Trend) is considered by many to be one of the bigest gas plays ever found in North America," said Tom Woods, an analyst with the Washington-based Gas Research Institute.

Based on results of three exploration wells drilled by the San Francisco-based company, analysts estimated Chevron's Destin Dome project could yield as much as 1 trillion cubic feet of gas trapped more than 20,000 feet below the surface of the earth.
"God generally doesn't make these kinds of fields orphans. They generally have a lot of large brothers and sisters," Woods said.

But before a production permit can be issued, state and federal regulators must sign off on Chevron's plan to drill new wells and build platforms and pipelines to ship gas back to processing plants in Mobile, Ala., starting in 1999.

Florida currently enforces a de facto moratorium on drilling off its Atlantic coast and in waters off the Gulf coast south of Venice, Fla. The state's Congressional delegation also blocked federal regulators from selling new drilling leases within 100 miles of the state's beaches.

"(Existing leaseholders) could move forward for exploration and other activities, but that would be it. There are no new leases that are coming up," said Carliane Johnson, a regulator with the Florida Bureau of Geology.

But more than 100 leases remain active in the waters off Florida's Gulf coast, including 64 in the area where Chevron and its partners, Conoco Inc. and Murphy Exploration and Production Co., control 11 tracts over the Destin Dome.

While Chevron wages its battle to drill in federal waters, Coastal Petroleum Corp., a subsidiary of Bermuda-based Coastal Caribbean Oil and Minerals Inc., is one court judgment away from winning a permit to sink a well in state waters 10 miles south of St. George Island off the Florida panhandle. (Corrects to show that Coastal Petroleum is a subsidiary of Bermuda-based Coastal Caribbean Oil and Minerals Inc, and is not a subsidiary of Houston's Coastal Corp).

The company holds leases dating back to World War II along 425 miles of Florida Gulf coastline from Apalachicola south to Naples, but has been stymied by state regulators opposed to offshore drilling.

If Coastal and Chevron win drilling rights, several major oil companies are expected to jump into the waters off the coast of Florida. "I'm sure the other companies are looking to see what happens with Chevron," Johnson said.
Environmentalists already are geared up to battle the oil companies, and blasted Chevron for quietly filing its drilling request hours before offices closed for the Thanksgiving Day holiday.
"It doesn't surprise me that they issued it the day before the start of a long weekend," said Jacobson, campaign director with the Tallahasee-based environmental group.
